summary: Describes version 0 of the Ogg bitstream format, a freely available container that can hold any number of audio, video, and other data streams in one stream. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A lunchbox can hold a sandwich, fruit, and a drink together. Ogg is a free box like that for sound, pictures, and other data, so they travel as a single file.

questions: how does ogg page header work
what is ogg chaining and grouping
subtitle: A free container format that interleaves audio, video and other streams in pages with built-in sync and seeking.

tldr.problem: Media streams from different codecs need a generic way to be framed, interleaved, checked for corruption and seeked, with little overhead and without intellectual property concerns.
tldr.mechanism: Ogg splits each codec packet into 255-byte segments, groups segments into variable-size pages with a header and CRC checksum, and interleaves pages of several logical bitstreams into one physical bitstream.
tldr.outcome: Version 0 of the format is documented as an Informational RFC. It is codec-independent, with each codec defined by its own media mapping such as Ogg Vorbis.

today: RFC 3533 is an Informational RFC describing Ogg version 0. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its companion for the MIME type is RFC 3534.

sections.title: What Ogg Is For
sections.content:
The Ogg bitstream format was developed as part of a project to create freely available and freely re-implementable codecs. The Xiph.Org developers intend it to be usable without intellectual property concerns.

Ogg provides framing, error protection and a seeking structure for higher-level codec streams made of raw data packets, such as the Vorbis audio codec. It can interleave different binary media and other time-continuous streams, and lets a reader split them back into the encoder's original packets without decoding to find the boundaries.

The design requirements include framing, interleaving, detection of corruption, recapture after a parsing error, position landmarks for random access, streaming capability, simplicity, easy concatenation, and no more than approximately 1-2% overhead. The MIME type application/ogg is registered with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: Ogg is one big box that can carry music, video and other things at once. It has little markers so you can jump into the middle or recover if part of it gets damaged.

sections.title: Logical and Physical Bitstreams
sections.content:
The result of encapsulation is the physical bitstream. It holds one or more logical bitstreams, each made by one encoder and cut into packets meaningful only to that encoder. Here "packet" does not mean a network packet.

Pages from different logical bitstreams are interleaved in the physical bitstream. Each logical bitstream is identified by a serial number in each page header, created randomly. Each starts with a bos page (beginning of stream) and ends with an eos page (end of stream). The bos page identifies the codec, and by convention starts with magic data. For Ogg Vorbis it starts with byte 0x01 followed by vorbis, 7 bytes in total.

Ogg knows two kinds of multiplexing. Grouping interleaves several logical bitstreams, for example video with audio tracks, and all their bos pages MUST come together at the start. Chaining concatenates complete physical bitstreams one after another. Ogg has no concept of time, only unitless increasing granule positions, so a media mapping defines synchronisation.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a train with cars from different companies. Each car has a label for who owns it, and the train can be joined to another train end to end.

sections.title: From Packets to Pages
sections.content:
Packets can be any size. Because pages have a maximum size of about 64 kBytes, Ogg divides each packet into 255-byte chunks plus a final shorter chunk, called segments. Segments are only logical and have no header of their own.

A group of contiguous segments is wrapped in a page. The page header holds a segment table of lacing values. A value of 255 means another value follows for the same packet, a value under 255 ends the packet, and a packet that is a multiple of 255 bytes is ended by a lacing value of 0. A zero-length packet is not an error.

The scheme is optimized for packets between 50 and 200 bytes. Small packets get the minimum byte-aligned overhead of 1 byte, and large packets (over 512 bytes) see a fairly constant ~0.5% overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Big messages are cut into equal-sized slices with a short last slice, then slices are packed into envelopes. A small note on the envelope says how long each slice is.

sections.title: The Ogg Page Header
sections.content:
Pages are variable in size, usually 4-8 kB, with a maximum of 65307 bytes. Each is self-contained, so a decoder can verify a single page at a time. The header begins with the capture pattern OggS (0x4f 0x67 0x67 0x53), which helps a decoder find page boundaries and regain sync after corruption.

  • stream_structure_version: 1 byte, 0 for this document.
  • header_type_flag: 1 byte; bit 0x01 marks a continued packet, 0x02 the first page (bos) and 0x04 the last page (eos).
  • granule_position: 8 bytes of codec-dependent position; -1 means no packet finishes on this page.
  • bitstream_serial_number: 4 bytes.
  • page_sequence_number: 4 bytes, so a decoder can spot page loss.
  • CRC_checksum: 4 bytes, a 32 bit CRC with generator polynomial 0x04c11db7.
  • number_page_segments: 1 byte, followed by the segment table of that many bytes.

The header size is number_page_segments + 27 bytes. Multi-byte fields are encoded least significant byte first.
sections.plainLanguage: Every envelope starts with the secret word OggS, then who it belongs to, its number in line, and a check number to spot damage.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Ogg is only a container. It provides no generic encryption or signing of itself or its contents, but it can carry encrypted and signed content, and an external mechanism can encrypt or sign a whole physical bitstream.

Because it carries binary data, an Ogg bitstream could include executable content, which the RFC says Ogg itself does not make a threat. Applications decoding Ogg must correctly handle manipulated bitstreams and buffer overflows.
sections.plainLanguage: The box does not lock what is inside. Whoever opens it must be careful about what is in there and about boxes that were tampered with.

fields.name: capture_pattern
fields.desc: Magic number OggS marking the start of a page.

fields.name: version
fields.desc: Version of the Ogg file format; 0 here.

fields.name: header_type
fields.desc: Flags: continued packet 0x01, first page 0x02, last page 0x04.

fields.name: granule_position
fields.desc: Codec-dependent position hint; -1 if no packet finishes on the page.

fields.name: page_sequence_number
fields.desc: Lets the decoder identify page loss.

fields.name: CRC_checksum
fields.desc: 32 bit CRC of the page, generator polynomial 0x04c11db7.

fields.name: page_segments
fields.desc: Number of entries in the segment table that follows.
